Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: Mariana had spent three decades as a detective, but nothing prepared her for the call that Saturday evening-a clandestine drug lab explosion in a warehouse on the south side. She arrived before the hazmat team, pushing through a crowd of panicked neighbors to reach a collapsed wall. A cloud of acrid fumes hit her as she knelt to check for survivors; her lungs seized, and she gasped, tasting something metallic and chemical. She felt her own sweat pooling under her vest, the sour smell mixing with the burning plastic. A paramedic later guided her to an ambulance, where the sterile antiseptic and latex gloves burned into her memory. That night in the emergency room, the doctors told her the chemicals were unstable but she would recover. Mariana did breathe again, but not the way she used to. In the weeks that followed, she found herself ducking into doorways whenever she heard a sudden bang-a truck backfiring, a dropped metal tray in the precinct break room. Her body stayed tense, her shoulders knotted, her eyes darting across the parking lot before she got out of her car. What frightened her most was the way the hospital smell would catch her off guard. The first time she walked past a clinic, her throat tightened, and she had to cover her face with both hands, forcing herself to think of the grocery list instead. Even a colleague's sweat after a morning run made her stomach drop and her mind leap back to that warehouse floor, but only in jagged pieces-a flash of a chemical drum, the paramedic's glove, the cold oxygen mask-never the whole thing. She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that her body would always be this coiled, that the department that sent her in without proper gear had failed her entirely. Once she was convinced that the world and her own body were no longer safe, nearly every ordinary sound or smell became a trigger - a car backfiring, a whiff of bleach, a colleague's aftershave - because her appraisals had turned the everyday into a landscape of potential threats. That belief kept her tethered to the explosion scene, as if her mind needed to revisit the exact moment where normal ended, so the memory stayed close and vivid. That last belief made her flinch every time she saw a uniform, so she started avoiding the squad room, taking paperwork home, speaking only to her partner through text. The connections tightened into a loop she could not name. A sudden sound put her on high alert and, at the same time, shoved a fragmented memory into her throat; she blocked it before it finished, and the very act of blocking convinced her she was losing control of her own mind. The more she believed she had to be on guard all the time, the more she scanned the hallway for shadows, and the more she scanned, the more breathless she became when she caught the faintest hint of a cleaning product. That breathlessness sent her straight to her old redirection trick-picturing her daughter's graduation-but the trick also reinforced her sense that the memory was too dangerous to face. She had started hiding her face at her desk whenever a nurse's perfume drifted by, and in those moments the event felt present again, not over. Each time she pushed the memory away, the negative appraisal that she was permanently broken grew stronger, and that appraisal made her avoid not only smells but also authority figures: she no longer attended briefings with the captain, citing a stomach bug. But that blocking had the unintended effect of keeping the memory intact and unprocessed, so that when it next surfaced it arrived with a force she could not counter - all that suppression had preserved it in full. Her work suffered-she missed a deadline on a burglary case-and her partner gently asked if she was okay. She said she was fine, but she was certain she was not. What finally brought Mariana to seek help was a piece of evidence: a forensic photo from a new case, a chemical spill at a manufacturing plant. The image alone triggered a surge of breathlessness so intense she thought she would black out. She drove herself to the precinct's employee assistance office, her hands shaking on the wheel. What she hoped for was to stop the loop-to be able to walk into the break room without covering her face, to hear a door slam without her heart racing. But what she feared most was that the loop would not break, that the institutional failure she blamed would never be fixed, and that the woman who used to lead scenes would remain fractured, always on guard, always bracing for a trigger she could not predict. Each time a trigger struck like that, it drove the conviction deeper that she would never feel normal again and that her body was permanently wired for alarm.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that triggers directly cause negative appraisals; triggers cause memory, threat, or maladaptive strategies, but not appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause memory; negative appraisals are consequences of strategies or memory, not vice versa.
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause triggers; appraisals may influence perception but not cause the external triggering stimuli.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies directly cause memory; strategies are used to suppress or avoid memory, not to produce it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers directly cause negative appraisals; triggers cause memory, threat, or maladaptive strategies, but not appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause memory; negative appraisals are consequences of strategies or memory, not vice versa.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause triggers; appraisals may influence perception but not cause the external triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies directly cause memory; strategies are used to suppress or avoid memory, not to produce it.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
